input: This memo considers the question of whether maintenance sensors should be installed on the pumps at the plant, where 260 pumps are currently in operation. Maintenance records covering a period of 12 months show a total of 1356 h of unplanned downtime, and a closer look at those records reveals that bearing failures account for 51% of the downtime hours, which suggests that bearing condition is a particularly important part of the overall picture. A sensor set covering all 260 pumps has been quoted at $449k installed, together with a further $60k per year. In a vendor trial carried out on a comparable unit, the sensors were reported to cut downtime by 28%, although it should be noted that this figure is a vendor figure and was not measured at this plant. As an alternative to immediate full installation, a pilot on 19 pumps would cost $32k over three months. It should also be noted that spare-part lead times are unchanged by the sensors. By comparison, full installation would commit $449k immediately, plus a further $60k per year, in return for a downtime reduction that has not yet been demonstrated at this plant. On balance, this memo recommends the three-month pilot; the reliability engineering group owns the pilot and will report before the March capital review, and the decision on full installation is held until the pilot results have been reported and considered.
target:
The reliability engineering group should run the three-month pilot of the maintenance sensors on 19 pumps, and report before the March capital review; the decision on full installation is held until the pilot results are reported.

Maintenance records for 12 months show 1356 h of unplanned downtime across the 260 pumps at the plant, and bearing failures account for 51% of the downtime hours. A sensor set for all 260 pumps is quoted at $449k installed, plus $60k per year. In a vendor trial on a comparable unit the sensors cut downtime by 28%; the figure is a vendor figure and was not measured at this plant. The pilot costs $32k over three months, against a full installation at $449k plus $60k per year whose downtime saving at this plant is unmeasured. Spare-part lead times are unchanged by the sensors, and the pilot does not alter them.

The pilot pumps are drawn from the population that produced the recorded downtime, so the trial measures the failure modes the records identify rather than a selected subset. Bearing failures dominate the downtime hours, and bearing condition is what the sensors monitor; the pilot therefore tests the sensors against the plant's largest downtime source. The report to the capital review states the downtime change on the pilot pumps over the trial, the false-alarm rate the maintenance crews worked under, and any downtime the sensors themselves caused. The pilot tests the vendor figure on plant equipment and plant failure history; the full-installation decision takes the pilot's measured downtime change as its evidence.
